The missing story of the 2014 election

Recently, I read an article stating that the Republican wave was just beginning. In 2016, Republicans will win more Senate seat. I took at look at the 2016 Senate map. I was not impressed. This early, I am expecting Democrats to pick up seats in 2016. But it is really early.

This article claims that Democrats will have a lock on the Presidency.

The Blue Wall is block of states that no Republican Presidential candidate can realistically hope to win. Tuesday that block finally extended to New Hampshire, meaning that at the outset of any Presidential campaign, a minimally effective Democratic candidate can expect to win 257 electoral votes without even trying. That’s 257 out of the 270 needed to win.

While this is an interesting analysis, maybe not so much has changed. Five of the last six apparently legitimate elections won by Republicans were won by those who came from California -- precisely a state behind that "blue wall." I am sure Republicans are taking notice.

In the meantime, there is a very nice right-wing Democratic governor in New York who appears ready to step in while Republicans get their ducks in a row.

It really is interesting, isn't it? It also seems unduly pessimistic. As you point out, it is really early yet to be making a call like this. I think it might even be a bit of a stretch to call it a possible trend. Not that it would be wise of the Republicans to rest on their electoral laurels anyway.

Something, some force, some gathering of sane, rational, authentically concerned human beings generally at peace with reality must emerge in the next four to six years from the right, or our opportunity will be lost for a long generation.

That is simply not going to happen. People who get to know me politically, or who read my political ideals elsewhere, are generally surprised to discover that I'm a conservative because

  1. I don't just make up convenient bullshit
  2. I recognize that we've become a constitutional oligarchy
  3. I'm concerned about workers' rights and compensation

For those three things, I'm usually accused of being an unemployed, long-haired, scraggly, pot-smoking hippie up until I reveal that I'm a conservative and explain that

1) Only a deity can simply declare a desired reality

2) We're an oligarchy because the populace is by and large too uninformed to contribute politically

3) Undervaluing our workers contradicts the "work to get ahead" conservative ideal

This anecdote isn't only my anecdote. It's shared by every single moderate conservative not intermittently beating a drum for war, not focusing primarily on anti-Obama sentiment, and not distracted by climate change denial to the point of uselessness. So, once Obama's term is up, the political landscape is more nuanced (especially considering recent stories about Russia), and climate change deniers are mocked off the stage, the people controlling the GOP will be absolutely irrelevant. And the rest of us will have been disenfranchised and insulted for so long, that I wouldn't be surprised if many conservatives feel exactly the same way that I do right now...

Fuck the GOP. Big tent theory corrupted it, the Tea Party infected it, and its prognosis is terminal.

And the most ironic thing of all is that the one and only republican with a voice who has said anything that could have averted this is also one of the worst of the bunch: Bobby Jindal, when he said that the GOP should stop being the party of stupid.

Now if only this could yet be discussed anywhere but on this site without it leading to accusations of being anti-capitalist or questions about what I do for a living, as if thinking that either is appropriate or follows could even make sense to a schizophrenic, syphilitic brain.

I feel your pain, in a way. For quite a few years, I was a Republican and conservative leaning. (I still have my twitches, heh) But for many of the reasons you list here, among others, I started examining where I stood under that big tent, and I realized that my place was actually outside of it. There are many Republicans I know that increasingly feel that the GOP doesn't really represent their interests or beliefs any longer. Whether or not that disenchantment will ultimately lead to the demise of the party is a whole other kettle of fish entirely. Most folks will probably hold their noses and vote R at the end of the day, because while the Republicans aren't doing it for them, they're still not on board with the Democrats, either. In any event, as I said above, I think declaring the Democrats have a lock on 2016 is pretty premature.

It is definitely premature, but if it's business as usual with the GOP for the next two years then it's going to be premature and accurate. The first thing the GOP should be considering is winning back some of the youth because if it doesn't, then the party is biologically limited to an expiration date. To do that will require bold compromise and a willingness to reconsider policy in a manner that is difficult for any party with bolshevist principles.

They're taking the right steps, gradually, by taking their time reconsidering marijuana policy and leaning toward legalization. That issue has long been treated as the stuff of hippies and the far left, but if you actually stop and think about what conservatism is, prohibition is liberal. It's a fiscally irresponsible affront to liberty that accomplishes absolutely nothing except increasing the size and waste of government.

Current hot button issues regarding the Internet should also see the GOP siding with the majority of young people. So the President pays lip service to that way of thinking while it was he who put the Internet in danger to begin with. That reveals another issue the GOP needs to overcome: When your central tenet is to oppose somebody, they can define everything else about you. The GOP is getting played by Obama.

Republicans have a smorgasbord of opportunities to bolster their foreign policy and national security attitude now, but they're ignoring it. When McCain was running for President, Palin was laughed at by the nation for her talk about Russia and McCain's concerns earned eye rolls. Surprise! We have a delicate situation involving Russia violating the sovereignty of their neighbor while the GOP pretends it's too good to say, "We told you so."

I'm not one for opportunistic politics, but it's not as if the GOP ever shies away from that with their Benghazi hearings and Obamacare circus. So, are they a two trick pony and that's it? Or is it three tricks? They do seem to have no qualms about damaging the economy by shutting down government for the sake of obstructionism. So, while criticizing a generation in regard to working hard and being responsible about long term planning, they seem to be blinded to everything an inch past their nose.

They need to get humble, get realistic, get personable, and get smart. If they can do that, then they will have the White House and it would be as premature yet certain to announce that as it is to say they won't if it's business as usual. It's time for the pendulum to swing their way, and if it doesn't then it's going to be a signal to them and everybody else that their party is irrelevant, ineffectual, and on its way out.

At least the Kochs have had the cowardice to trojan their bought Tea Party into the GOP. Had they the foresight to let the party stand on its own, of its own merit (or lack thereof), then we'd be stuck with them if the GOP fails.

I bet GOP strategists are quick to point out that history doesn't favor three democrat terms in the White House in a row. I wonder if they're wise enough that the histrionics don't make them complacent. "It's okay! Karl Rove will throw money at it! That worked so well the last two times!"
